events.title: A V-2 rocket is launched successfully for the first time
events.summary: Germany's ballistic missile is the forerunner of modern space rockets.
events.description: On October 3, 1942, Germany successfully launched the V-2 for the first time. Developed from 1936 by scientists led by Wernher von Braun, it was a ballistic missile and the forerunner of modern space rockets. About 5,000 people died in V-2 attacks, and at least 10,000 prisoners from the Mittelbau-Dora concentration camp died as forced labour building V-2s. On June 20, 1944, a V-2 became the first rocket to reach space.

sources.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica - V-2 rocket

events.title: The Madrid Protocol is signed to protect Antarctica
events.summary: Nations agree to designate Antarctica a natural reserve devoted to peace and science.
events.description: On October 4, 1991, the Protocol on Environmental Protection to the Antarctic Treaty was signed in Madrid. It designates Antarctica as a "natural reserve, devoted to peace and science" and prohibits all activities relating to Antarctic mineral resources except scientific research. It entered into force in 1998.

sources.name: Secretariat of the Antarctic Treaty - The Protocol on Environmental Protection to the Antarctic Treaty

events.title: Parisians march on Versailles
events.summary: The crowd that follows brings the royal family back to Paris.
events.description: On October 5, 1789, Parisians marched to Versailles after the king refused to sanction the August decrees abolishing feudalism and the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen. The next day they brought the royal family back to Paris, and the National Constituent Assembly followed the court there.

sources.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica - French Revolution: Events of 1789

events.title: The Wright brothers make a record flight in Flyer No. 3
events.summary: A flight of about 24 miles shows the airplane is ready for practical use.
events.description: On October 5, 1905, the Wright brothers made a record flight of about 24 miles in their new Flyer No. 3 at Huffman Prairie near Dayton, Ohio. In 1904 about 100 flights had totaled only 45 minutes in the air. The Smithsonian says the Wrights now had a practical airplane; they turned to securing a patent and finding a buyer, and did not fly at all in 1906 and 1907.

sources.name: National Park Service - Wright Brothers
National Air and Space Museum - You Just Invented the Airplane, Now What?

events.title: The Moulin Rouge opens in Montmartre
events.summary: The Paris music hall launches the French cancan to fame.
events.description: On October 6, 1889, the Moulin Rouge opened at Place Blanche in Paris. Founders Joseph Oller and Charles Zidler nicknamed it the first Women Palace and promised a temple of music and dance. The French cancan became its centerpiece, with La Goulue as its figurehead, and Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec, a regular, made seventeen paintings inspired by the venue.

sources.name: Moulin Rouge (official site) - The great periods
Encyclopaedia Britannica - Moulin Rouge

events.title: The Stamp Act Congress meets in New York
events.summary: Delegates from nine colonies protest taxation without representation.
events.description: On October 7, 1765, delegates from nine American colonies met in New York City to answer the Stamp Act. It was the first time representatives of the colonies had gathered and acted collectively. Its Declaration of Rights and Grievances, approved October 19, held that no taxes may be imposed on the colonists but with their own consent, given through their representatives.

sources.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica - Stamp Act Congress
National Constitution Center - On this day: No taxation without representation!
Americans at War (via Encyclopedia.com) - Stamp Act Congress

events.title: US-led strikes against the Taliban begin in Afghanistan
events.summary: The campaign opens weeks after the September 11 attacks.
events.description: On October 7, 2001, President George W. Bush announced that the United States military had begun strikes against al Qaeda training camps and Taliban military installations in Afghanistan, in an operation named Enduring Freedom. He said the Taliban had ignored demands to close terrorist camps and hand over al Qaeda leaders, and that food and medicine would also be dropped to Afghans.

sources.name: George W. Bush White House Archives - Presidential Address to the Nation, October 7, 2001

events.title: Corporal Alvin York captures 132 German soldiers
events.summary: A Tennessee blacksmith turns a patrol's disaster into a Medal of Honor action.
events.description: On October 8, 1918, during the Meuse-Argonne Offensive, Corporal Alvin York took command of his patrol near Châtel-Chéhéry, France, after heavy casualties. He silenced a German machine-gun nest and captured four officers and 128 men. York, a Tennessee blacksmith who had been denied conscientious objector status, received the Medal of Honor in April 1919.

sources.name: Congressional Medal of Honor Society - Alvin Cullium York
Encyclopaedia Britannica - Alvin York

events.title: A landslide wave overtops Italy's Vaiont Dam
events.summary: The wave nearly wipes out the town of Longarone below.
events.description:
On October 9, 1963, an estimated 260 million cubic metres of rock broke free from Monte Toc and fell into the reservoir behind the Vaiont Dam in Italy. The slide sent a wave 150 to 200 metres above the dam, over its crest and down the narrow valley below.

The town of Longarone, almost directly below the dam, was nearly completely destroyed, and about 2,000 people died. The dam itself was largely unaffected and still stands, but its reservoir has never been refilled.

sources.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica - Vaiont Dam

events.title: Malala Yousafzai is shot by a Taliban gunman
events.summary: The schoolgirl who campaigned for girls' education survives and keeps speaking out.
events.description:
On October 9, 2012, Malala Yousafzai was shot in the head by a gunman from the Tehreek-e Taliban Pakistan (TTP) as she was travelling home from school. Under the name Gul Makai, she had written a diary for BBC Urdu about daily life as the group restricted girls' schooling in Pakistan.

She survived after treatment in Birmingham, England, and continued her campaign for girls' education. In 2014, at 17, she was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize, becoming the youngest Nobel laureate at the time.

sources.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica - Malala Yousafzai

events.title: Afghans vote in their first direct presidential election
events.summary: Hamid Karzai wins more than half of some eight million votes.
events.description:
On October 9, 2004, Afghans voted for a president under a new constitution, approved that January, which called for a directly elected head of state. Hamid Karzai, who had led the interim administration since late December 2001, won more than 55 percent of an estimated eight million votes.

More than 40 percent of the voters were women. The United States congratulated Karzai as Afghanistan's first democratically elected leader, and he was sworn into office later that year.

sources.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica - Hamid Karzai
Voice of America - Karzai Goals for Afghanistan (editorial, November 8, 2004)

events.title: The Tokyo Olympics open, the first Games held in Asia
events.summary: More than 5,000 athletes from 93 countries gather in Tokyo.
events.description:
On October 10, 1964, the Summer Olympic Games opened in Tokyo, the first time the Olympics were held in Asia. More than 5,000 athletes from 93 countries competed until October 24.

The Tokyo Games added volleyball and judo to the programme and were the first to use computers to keep statistics. South Africa did not take part, having been banned by the IOC for its policy of apartheid.

sources.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica - Tokyo 1964 Olympic Games

events.title: Spiro Agnew resigns as U.S. vice president
events.summary: He leaves office while pleading no contest to a tax charge.
events.description:
On October 10, 1973, Spiro T. Agnew resigned as vice president of the United States. He pleaded nolo contendere (no contest) to a single federal count of failing to report $29,500 of income he had received in 1967, and he was fined $10,000 and sentenced to three years of unsupervised probation.

He was the second person to resign the vice presidency. The first, John C. Calhoun, had stepped down in 1832.

sources.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica - Spiro T. Agnew

events.title: The Partial Test Ban Treaty enters into force
events.summary: Nuclear tests in the air, in space and underwater are banned.
events.description:
On October 10, 1963, the treaty banning nuclear weapons tests in the atmosphere, in outer space and underwater entered into force. The United States, the Soviet Union and the United Kingdom had signed it in Moscow on August 5, and the U.S. Senate had ratified it on September 24.

The treaty still allowed underground tests and set up no inspection system. More than 100 other governments signed within a few months, with France and China the notable exceptions. It did not reduce nuclear stockpiles or halt the production of nuclear weapons.

sources.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica - Nuclear Test-Ban Treaty
Atomic Heritage Foundation - Limited or Partial Test Ban Treaty

events.title: William Lassell discovers Neptune's moon Triton
events.summary: The moon is found just 17 days after Neptune itself.
events.description:
On October 10, 1846, the British astronomer William Lassell discovered Triton, just 17 days after the planet Neptune itself had been found. Triton is about 2,700 kilometres (1,680 miles) across.

It is the only large moon in the solar system that orbits in the opposite direction to its planet's rotation. When Voyager 2 flew past in 1989, it found active geysers and surface temperatures of about -235°C (-391°F), among the coldest in the solar system.

sources.name: NASA Science - Triton

events.title: The Netherlands Antilles is dissolved
events.summary: Curaçao and Sint Maarten become countries within the Dutch kingdom.
events.description:
On October 10, 2010, a constitutional reform of the Kingdom of the Netherlands dissolved the Netherlands Antilles, a grouping of five Caribbean islands. Curaçao and Sint Maarten became autonomous countries within the kingdom, while Bonaire, Sint Eustatius and Saba became public entities of the Netherlands itself.

Aruba had already left the Netherlands Antilles in 1986. Since 2010 the kingdom has consisted of four countries: the Netherlands, Aruba, Curaçao and Sint Maarten.

sources.name: Statistics Netherlands (CBS) - The Dutch Caribbean 15 years after the dissolution of the Netherlands Antilles

events.title: Kathryn Sullivan becomes the first American woman to walk in space
events.summary: She spends three and a half hours outside the shuttle Challenger.
events.description:
On October 11, 1984, during the Space Shuttle Challenger's STS-41G mission, Kathryn D. Sullivan became the first American woman to walk in space. With fellow astronaut David C. Leestma, she spent three hours and 29 minutes outside the shuttle, where Leestma showed that satellites could be refuelled in orbit and Sullivan stowed a malfunctioning antenna.

She was not the first woman to do so: the Soviet cosmonaut Svetlana Savitskaya had walked in space that July. Sullivan later led the U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, and in 2020 she became the first woman to descend to the Challenger Deep, the deepest point in the ocean.

sources.name: NASA - Kathryn Sullivan: The First American Woman to Walk in Space
Encyclopaedia Britannica - Kathryn Sullivan

events.title: Saturday Night Live airs for the first time
events.summary: George Carlin hosts the first show and does no sketches at all.
events.description:
On October 11, 1975, NBC broadcast the first episode of what became Saturday Night Live, hosted by the comedian George Carlin. Instead of acting in sketches, Carlin performed four stand-up monologues, between music from Billy Preston and Janis Ian and a short film by Albert Brooks.

The show was created by Lorne Michaels with Dick Ebersol, and its first cast, the "Not Ready for Primetime Players," included Dan Aykroyd, John Belushi, Chevy Chase, Jane Curtin, Garrett Morris, Laraine Newman and Gilda Radner. It became one of the longest-running programs in television and has won 90 Emmys.

sources.name: NBC Insider - George Carlin hosted the first SNL episode
Encyclopaedia Britannica - Saturday Night Live

events.title: Anita Hill testifies at Clarence Thomas's confirmation hearings
events.summary: Her televised account of harassment grips the nation.
events.description:
On October 11, 1991, the law professor Anita Hill testified before the Senate Judiciary Committee that Supreme Court nominee Clarence Thomas had made unwanted sexual advances and lewd comments when she worked for him. She faced a panel of 14 male senators, led by Joe Biden, and skeptical, often hostile questioning.

Thomas was narrowly confirmed, 52 to 48. The hearings raised public awareness of sexual harassment at work, and in the 1992 "Year of the Woman" the number of women in Congress roughly doubled.

sources.name: ABC News - Anita Hill reflects on Clarence Thomas testimony
Encyclopaedia Britannica - Anita Hill

events.title: Theodore Roosevelt becomes the first U.S. president to fly
events.summary: The former president circles a St. Louis airfield twice in a few minutes.
events.description:
On October 11, 1910, former president Theodore Roosevelt went up with the aviator Archibald Hoxsey during the International Aviation Meet at Kinloch Field outside St. Louis, Missouri. The two men circled the airfield twice in "three minutes and twenty seconds."

Roosevelt was no longer in office, so the first president to fly was a former one. Franklin D. Roosevelt later became the first sitting president to travel by airplane.

sources.name: White House Historical Association - The Wings of Franklin Roosevelt

events.title: Suicide bombers attack the USS Cole in Yemen
events.summary: Bombers in a small boat strike a U.S. Navy destroyer in Aden harbour.
events.description:
On October 12, 2000, suicide bombers steered a small boat into the side of the U.S. Navy destroyer USS Cole in the harbour of Aden, Yemen. The explosion killed 17 sailors and wounded 39.

The attackers were militants associated with al-Qaeda. The damaged ship was later carried away aboard the heavy transport ship MV Blue Marlin.

sources.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica - USS Cole attack

events.title: Bombs kill 202 people on the Indonesian island of Bali
events.summary: The attacks on two packed nightspots kill 88 Australians.
events.description:
At about 11 p.m. on October 12, 2002, bombs exploded at Paddy's pub and outside the Sari Club on Jalan Legian in Bali, Indonesia, and a third went off near the U.S. consulate. The attacks killed 202 people, including 88 Australians.

They were carried out by Jemaah Islamiah, a Southeast Asian militant group inspired by and linked to al-Qaeda.

sources.name: ABC News (Australia) - The Bali bombings killed 202 people and changed Australia

events.title: Edith Cavell is executed in German-occupied Brussels
events.summary: The British nurse had helped about 200 Allied soldiers escape.
events.description:
On October 12, 1915, the British nurse Edith Cavell was shot by a German firing squad in Brussels, together with Philippe Baucq. As matron of the Berkendael Institute, she had joined an underground network that helped British, French and Belgian soldiers reach the Netherlands, and about 200 men had been aided before her arrest in August 1915.

Her court-martial was considered legally valid, but the Allies publicised her execution widely, and it caused outrage abroad.

sources.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica - Edith Cavell

events.title: Pakistan's army ousts Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif
events.summary: Sharif tries to fire his army chief, and the army takes power instead.
events.description:
On October 12, 1999, Pakistani Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif dismissed the army chief, General Pervez Musharraf, while Musharraf was out of the country, and tried to stop the plane carrying him home from landing at Karachi airport. The armed forces took control of the airport and other government installations and deposed Sharif.

Musharraf headed the military government that followed and took the presidency in early 2001. He announced his resignation in August 2008.

sources.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica - Pervez Musharraf

events.title: Congress votes to put armed ships to sea
events.summary: The Continental Congress takes its first step toward an American navy.
events.description: On October 13, 1775, the Continental Congress voted to fit out ships for the war against Britain. A Marine Committee, appointed later, sent the first Continental squadron to sea under the command of Esek Hopkins, with orders to capture munitions.

sources.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica - United States Navy

events.title: Boston wins the first modern World Series
events.summary: Bill Dinneen's shutout settles the series against Pittsburgh.
events.description:
On October 13, 1903, the Boston Americans beat the Pittsburgh Pirates 3-0 at Boston's Huntington Avenue Grounds to win the first modern World Series, five games to three. Pitcher Bill Dinneen allowed only four hits and ended the game by striking out Honus Wagner.

The best-of-nine series between the American League and National League champions drew just over 100,000 fans, and each player's share of the receipts was slightly more than $1,000.

sources.name: Society for American Baseball Research - October 13, 1903: Big Bill Dinneen leads Boston to a triumph
Encyclopaedia Britannica - World Series

events.title: A plane carrying a Uruguayan rugby team crashes in the Andes
events.summary: Sixteen of the 45 people aboard survive more than two months in the mountains.
events.description:
On October 13, 1972, a Uruguayan Air Force plane carrying the Old Christians rugby team and others, 45 people in all, crashed high in the Andes.

More than two months later, two of the survivors, Roberto Canessa and Nando Parrado, trekked across the mountains for nine days until Parrado spotted horsemen across a river. He threw a note tied to a rock to a Chilean muleteer, Sergio Catalán, who alerted the authorities. By December 23, 1972, 16 men had been rescued.

sources.name: History Hit - How sixteen men survived the Andes flight disaster
History.com - Miracle of the Andes

events.title: Carbon dating places the Shroud of Turin in the Middle Ages
events.summary: Three laboratories date the linen to between 1260 and 1390.
events.description:
On October 13, 1988, Cardinal Anastasio Ballestrero of Turin announced that radiocarbon tests had dated the Shroud of Turin, with 95 percent certainty, to between 1260 and 1390. Laboratories at Oxford University, the University of Arizona and the Federal Institute of Technology in Zurich had each tested samples of the cloth.

The Vatican encouraged further scientific study and said Christians could continue to venerate the shroud as an image of Christ. The Holy See has made no official pronouncement on whether it is authentic.

sources.name: Biblical Archaeology Society - Has the Shroud of Turin been dated, finally?
Encyclopaedia Britannica - Shroud of Turin

events.title: Emperor Claudius dies and Nero takes power in Rome
events.summary: Roman tradition holds that his wife Agrippina poisoned him.
events.description:
On October 13, 54 CE, the Roman emperor Claudius died and was succeeded by Nero. Claudius had married his niece Agrippina and adopted her son, the future Nero, to the disadvantage of his own son Britannicus.

Roman tradition is unanimous that Agrippina poisoned Claudius, though the accounts differ on the details.

sources.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica - Claudius
Encyclopaedia Britannica - How did Claudius die?

events.title: Theodore Roosevelt is shot and gives his speech anyway
events.summary: A folded speech and a glasses case slow the bullet.
events.description:
On October 14, 1912, Theodore Roosevelt was shot outside the Hotel Gilpatrick in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, by John Flammang Schrank. The bullet was slowed by the folded 50-page manuscript of his speech and his eyeglass case before lodging in his chest wall.

Roosevelt went on to speak for about 80 minutes, telling the audience, "it takes more than that to kill a bull moose." Doctors decided not to remove the bullet, and he carried it for the rest of his life.

sources.name: Theodore Roosevelt Center - Why was Theodore Roosevelt shot?

events.title: Prisoners revolt at the Sobibor killing center
events.summary: About 300 people break out of the Nazi death camp.
events.description:
On October 14, 1943, prisoners at Sobibor, a German killing center, rose up. Led by Leon Feldhendler and Aleksandr (Sasha) Pechersky, they killed 11 German personnel and several guards, and about 300 of the roughly 600 prisoners still in the camp broke out.

About 100 were caught in the manhunt that followed, and some 50 escapees survived the war. The Germans then dismantled the camp, where at least 167,000 people had been killed since April 1942.

sources.name: United States Holocaust Memorial Museum - Sobibor

events.title: Winnie-the-Pooh is published
events.summary: A. A. Milne turns his son's nursery toys into a children's classic.
events.description:
On October 14, 1926, A. A. Milne's Winnie-the-Pooh was first published, with illustrations by E. H. Shepard. Milne based the stories on the nursery toys and games of his son, Christopher Robin, who appears in the book with Pooh, Piglet, Eeyore and their friends.

Their Hundred Acre Wood was modelled on Ashdown Forest in East Sussex, England. A second collection, The House at Pooh Corner, followed in 1928.

sources.name: The Conversation - Winnie-the-Pooh at 100
Encyclopaedia Britannica - Winnie-the-Pooh

events.title: Erwin Rommel is forced to take poison
events.summary: Hitler offers the "Desert Fox" poison instead of a trial.
events.description:
On October 14, 1944, the German field marshal Erwin Rommel died at Herrlingen, near Ulm, after taking poison. He had been implicated in the conspiracy against Hitler after the failed July Plot, and Hitler gave him the choice of taking poison, which would protect his family, or facing trial.

Rommel had been nicknamed "the Desert Fox" for his surprise attacks while commanding the Afrika Korps in North Africa. After his death he was buried with full military honours.

sources.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica - Erwin Rommel

events.title: Mata Hari is executed as a spy
events.summary: Doubts about the dancer's guilt have grown ever since.
events.description:
On October 15, 1917, Margaretha Geertruida Zelle, the Dutch-born dancer known as Mata Hari, was executed by a French firing squad at Vincennes. A French military court had found her guilty that July of spying for Germany during World War I.

She had taken German money as "agent H21" while also trying to work for France, but the investigating officer could not prove she had given the Germans useful information. Germany publicly cleared her in 1930, and French documents released in 2017 led many to see her as a scapegoat.

sources.name: Fries Museum - The real story of Mata Hari
Encyclopaedia Britannica - Was Mata Hari innocent?

events.title: The Black Panther Party is founded in Oakland
events.summary: Huey P. Newton and Bobby Seale start patrols against police brutality.
events.description:
On October 15, 1966, the college students Huey P. Newton and Bobby Seale founded the Black Panther Party for Self-Defense in West Oakland, California. Its first aim was to patrol African American neighbourhoods to protect residents from police brutality.

The party grew to more than 2,000 members with chapters in 48 states and ran community services such as the Free Breakfast for Children Program, begun in January 1969. FBI counterintelligence operations weakened it, and by the mid-1980s its activities had all but ceased.

sources.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica - Black Panther Party

events.title: I Love Lucy airs for the first time
events.summary: Lucille Ball and Desi Arnaz's sitcom is filmed before a live audience.
events.description:
On Monday evening, October 15, 1951, the first episode of I Love Lucy was broadcast, starring Lucille Ball and Desi Arnaz as a married couple, with Vivian Vance and William Frawley as their neighbours.

Its 180 half-hour episodes were performed before a live studio audience and captured on film, which allowed them to be rerun and helped keep the series popular long after it ended.

sources.name: Library of Congress - I Love Lucy: An American Legend

events.title: Napoleon reaches his final exile on St Helena
events.summary: After nine weeks at sea, the defeated emperor arrives at the remote island.
events.description:
On October 15, 1815, after nine weeks at sea aboard the Northumberland, Napoleon arrived at the island of St Helena, his place of exile after his defeat at Waterloo. Because his intended residence, Longwood, was not ready, he first lodged with the Balcombe family at a house called the Briars.

He moved to Longwood on December 10, 1815. He died on May 5, 1821, at the age of 51.

sources.name: Fondation Napoléon - From Waterloo to the island of St Helena

events.title: Thomas Sankara is killed in a coup in Burkina Faso
events.summary: The revolutionary leader who renamed his country dies at 37.
events.description:
On October 15, 1987, Thomas Sankara, the leader of Burkina Faso, was assassinated in Ouagadougou in a coup led by Blaise Compaoré. He was 37.

On the first anniversary of his rise to power, in August 1984, Sankara had renamed Upper Volta as Burkina Faso, "land of upright people." His government fought corruption, promoted women's rights, education and health care, and planted 10 million trees against desertification. In 2022 Compaoré and nine others were convicted of complicity in his murder.

sources.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica - Thomas Sankara

events.title: Marie-Antoinette is guillotined in Paris
events.summary: The former queen of France is executed two days after her trial.
events.description:
On October 16, 1793, Marie-Antoinette, the former queen of France, was guillotined in Paris at the age of 37. She had been brought before the Revolutionary Tribunal on October 14 and found guilty of crimes against the state.

Her enemies spread the story that, told the people had no bread, she replied "Let them eat cake." The remark is a legend, not an established quotation.

sources.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica - Marie-Antoinette

events.title: Jane Eyre is published under the name Currer Bell
events.summary: Charlotte Brontë hides behind a pen name, and her novel is an instant success.
events.description:
On October 16, 1847, Charlotte Brontë's novel Jane Eyre was published, less than eight weeks after it was accepted. It appeared under the pseudonym Currer Bell; the Brontë sisters used such names to keep their identity secret and avoid the special treatment they believed reviewers gave to women.

The book, narrated in the first person by an independent and self-reliant heroine, was an immediate success.

sources.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica - Charlotte Brontë
Encyclopaedia Britannica - Jane Eyre

events.title: John Brown raids the federal armory at Harpers Ferry
events.summary: The abolitionist hopes to arm a rising against slavery.
events.description:
On the night of October 16, 1859, the abolitionist John Brown and his followers seized the U.S. Armory and Arsenal and the Rifle Works at Harpers Ferry, then in Virginia. He hoped to use the weapons to arm a liberating army against slavery.

The raid lasted about a day and a half. Sixteen people were killed, including ten of Brown's men, and on October 18 U.S. Marines under Colonel Robert E. Lee captured Brown. He was convicted of treason against Virginia, murder and conspiring with enslaved people to rebel, and was hanged on December 2. One newspaper said the raid had "advanced the cause of disunion more than any other event" since the government's founding.

sources.name: National Park Service - John Brown's Raid

events.title: Margaret Sanger opens the first U.S. birth control clinic
events.summary: More than 100 women come on the first day in Brooklyn.
events.description:
On October 16, 1916, Margaret Sanger opened the first birth control clinic in the United States, in the Brownsville section of Brooklyn, New York. She ran it with her sister Ethel Byrne, a registered nurse, and the interpreter Fania Mindell, in open defiance of a New York law against distributing contraception.

The clinic served more than 100 women on its first day and some 400 before police arrested all three on October 26. Sanger served 30 days in jail, but her appeal led to a 1918 ruling that let New York physicians prescribe contraception for general health reasons.

sources.name: Margaret Sanger Papers Project (New York University) - Brownsville Clinic
Encyclopaedia Britannica - Margaret Sanger

events.title: China tests its first atomic bomb
events.summary: It becomes the fifth country with nuclear weapons.
events.description:
On October 16, 1964, China exploded its first atomic bomb, a uranium implosion device set off atop a 330-foot steel tower at the Lop Nur test base. It produced 22 kilotons of force and made China the fifth country to possess nuclear weapons, after the United States, the Soviet Union, the United Kingdom and France.

Shortly afterward China declared it would "never at any time and under any circumstances be the first to use nuclear weapons." It tested its first hydrogen bomb just 32 months later, on June 17, 1967.

sources.name: Atomic Heritage Foundation - Chinese Nuclear Program

events.title: Tommie Smith and John Carlos raise their fists on the Olympic podium
events.summary: Their protest in Mexico City gets them sent home from the Games.
events.description:
On October 16, 1968, at the Mexico City Olympics, Tommie Smith and John Carlos, gold and bronze medallists in the 200 metres, raised black-gloved fists on the podium to protest the mistreatment of African Americans. They stood shoeless to highlight Black poverty. Smith had won in 19.83 seconds, the first time the distance was run in under 20 seconds.

The U.S. Olympic Committee sent them home, and both received death threats. Smith later called it "the proudest moment" of his life and "one of the saddest."

sources.name: CBS News - Remembering 1968: Tommie Smith's raised fist salute
Encyclopaedia Britannica - Tommie Smith

events.title: Canada legalizes recreational cannabis
events.summary: Adults may now buy, carry and grow small amounts legally.
events.description:
On October 17, 2018, Canada's Cannabis Act came into force, legalizing and strictly regulating cannabis for adults. Depending on the province or territory, adults 18 or 19 and older could now possess up to 30 grams of dried legal cannabis in public and grow up to four plants per household.

The law created two new criminal offences, each carrying up to 14 years in jail: giving or selling cannabis to young people, and using a young person to commit a cannabis offence.

sources.name: Government of Canada - The Cannabis Act: The Facts

events.title: The English defeat the Scots at Neville's Cross
events.summary: Scotland's King David II is taken prisoner near Durham.
events.description:
On October 17, 1346, an English army defeated an invading Scottish force at Neville's Cross, near Durham in northern England. The Scots, allies of France, had invaded to draw Edward III's attention away from his siege of Calais during the Hundred Years' War.

Edward had left a strong force in the northern shires, and King David II of Scotland was captured in the battle. He remained a prisoner of the English until 1357.

sources.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica - Battle of Neville's Cross

events.title: The allied siege of Sevastopol begins
events.summary: British and French forces start an 11-month siege in the Crimean War.
events.description:
On October 17, 1854, British and French forces began the siege of Sevastopol, Russia's fortress and naval base in Crimea and the central objective of the Crimean War.

The siege lasted nearly a year. On September 11, 1855, three days after a successful French assault on the Malakhov strongpoint, the Russians blew up their forts, sank their ships and abandoned the city.

sources.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica - List of battles
Encyclopaedia Britannica - Crimean War

events.title: Mr. Smith Goes to Washington premieres before Congress
events.summary: Some senators in the audience are furious at how they are portrayed.
events.description:
On October 17, 1939, Frank Capra's Mr. Smith Goes to Washington had its premiere at Constitution Hall in Washington, D.C., with 45 senators and 250 members of the House in the audience. The film follows an idealistic freshman senator who stages a one-man filibuster against political corruption.

Most lawmakers responded well, but Senate Majority Leader Alben Barkley called it "silly and stupid" and said it showed the Senate as "a bunch of crooks."

sources.name: U.S. Senate - Mr. Smith Comes to Washington

events.title: U.S. diplomats urge seizing Cuba in the Ostend Manifesto
events.summary: Three ministers argue the U.S. should take Cuba if Spain will not sell it.
events.description:
On October 18, 1854, three U.S. diplomats, James Buchanan, John Y. Mason and Pierre Soulé, drew up a dispatch urging the United States to seize Cuba if Spain refused to sell it. The idea grew from fear of a slave revolt in Cuba like the one in Haiti and from a desire to expand U.S. slave territory.

The proposals were rejected, and when the dispatch became public, the Republican press branded it a "manifesto" aimed at Southern opinion. It marked the high point of the U.S. expansionist drive in the Caribbean in the 1850s.

sources.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica - Ostend Manifesto

events.title: The U.S. flag is raised over Puerto Rico
events.summary: The last Spanish troops sail home and the island passes to the United States.
events.description:
On October 18, 1898, the last Spanish troops sailed home from Puerto Rico and the U.S. flag was raised, completing a two-month handover that had begun on August 12. American troops had landed at Guánica Bay on July 25 during the Spanish-American War.

The Treaty of Paris, signed on December 10, 1898, formalized the transfer. The island was under military government until the Foraker Act set up a civilian government in 1900.

sources.name: Library of Congress - The World of 1898: Puerto Rico

events.title: The British Broadcasting Company is formed
events.summary: A group of radio makers creates the forerunner of today's BBC.
events.description:
On October 18, 1922, the British Broadcasting Company was established as a private corporation. Only genuine radio manufacturers could hold shares, and the company was funded by half of the 10-shilling licence fee on receivers plus a royalty on sales of radio sets.

John Reith ran it from the start. In 1927 it was replaced by a public body, the British Broadcasting Corporation, answerable to Parliament but run day to day by its Board of Governors, with Reith as director-general. The BBC kept its broadcasting monopoly until 1954.

sources.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica - Broadcasting: Formation of the British Broadcasting Company

events.title: Thomas Edison dies
events.summary: The inventor held a record 1,093 patents.
events.description:
On October 18, 1931, Thomas Edison died at West Orange, New Jersey, at the age of 84. He held a world-record 1,093 patents.

His inventions included the phonograph, the incandescent lamp, the carbon-button telephone transmitter and motion-picture equipment, along with the first commercial electric light and power system. His laboratory at Menlo Park is considered the first industrial research laboratory.

sources.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica - Thomas Edison

events.title: John Jay takes office as the first chief justice
events.summary: George Washington's pick swears his oaths in New York.
events.description:
On October 19, 1789, John Jay took his oaths as the first Chief Justice of the United States, before Richard Morris, chief justice of the State of New York.

President George Washington had nominated him on September 24, 1789, and the Senate confirmed him two days later.

sources.name: Supreme Court of the United States - Oaths Taken by the Chief Justices
Federal Judicial Center - Jay, John

events.title: Confederates raid St. Albans, Vermont, from Canada
events.summary: The northernmost action of the Civil War nets about $200,000.
events.description:
On October 19, 1864, about 25 Confederate soldiers who had been based in Canada raided St. Albans, Vermont. They robbed three banks of about $200,000, killed one man and fled back across the border.

Canadian authorities arrested about half of them on October 21 but released them on December 13, which caused strong protests in the United States. The dispute was still being argued in 1872, when a claims commission under the Treaty of Washington ruled against further American claims.

sources.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica - Saint Albans Raid

events.title: The First Battle of Ypres begins
events.summary: The fighting in Flanders ends the war of movement on the Western Front.
events.description:
On October 19, 1914, the First Battle of Ypres began in western Flanders, as German, British, French and Belgian forces each tried to outflank the other in the "race to the sea." The fighting lasted until November 22.

Neither side broke through, and both settled into the trench warfare that would mark the rest of the war. The British lost more than 54,000 killed, wounded and missing, the French at least 50,000, the Belgians more than 20,000, and the Germans more than 130,000.

sources.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica - First Battle of Ypres

events.title: Pope John Paul II beatifies Mother Teresa
events.summary: She is declared "Blessed" six years after her death in Calcutta.
events.description:
On October 19, 2003, Pope John Paul II beatified Mother Teresa of Calcutta, the founder of the Missionaries of Charity. Born Agnes Gonxha Bojaxhiu in Skopje in 1910, she had worked among the poor and dying of Calcutta, won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1979 and died there on September 5, 1997.

Pope Francis canonized her as St. Teresa of Calcutta on September 4, 2016.

sources.name: Vatican - Beatification of Mother Teresa of Calcutta, 19 October 2003
Encyclopaedia Britannica - Mother Teresa

events.title: Nixon has the Watergate special prosecutor fired
events.summary: The attorney general and his deputy resign rather than carry out the order.
events.description:
On October 20, 1973, President Richard Nixon ordered Attorney General Elliot Richardson to fire Archibald Cox, the special prosecutor investigating Watergate, who had subpoenaed the White House tapes. Richardson resigned rather than comply, and his deputy, William Ruckelshaus, also refused and left. Solicitor General Robert Bork finally dismissed Cox.

The firings became known as the Saturday Night Massacre. Under public pressure, Nixon agreed on October 23 to release tapes, and within a year the House Judiciary Committee had approved articles of impeachment. He announced his resignation on August 8, 1974.

sources.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica - Watergate scandal: Watergate trial and aftermath
Encyclopaedia Britannica - Saturday Night Massacre

events.title: A plane crash kills members of Lynyrd Skynyrd
events.summary: Singer Ronnie Van Zant dies when the band's plane runs out of fuel.
events.description:
On October 20, 1977, a plane carrying the Southern rock band Lynyrd Skynyrd ran out of fuel and crashed near Gillsburg, Mississippi. The crash killed lead singer Ronnie Van Zant, guitarist Steve Gaines, backup singer Cassie Gaines, assistant tour manager Dean Kilpatrick and both pilots. Twenty people survived, some critically injured.

The band broke up afterward. Surviving members reunited in 1987 with Ronnie's younger brother Johnny Van Zant as lead singer, and the band entered the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2006.

sources.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica - Lynyrd Skynyrd
Encyclopaedia Britannica - Ronnie Van Zant

events.title: Muammar al-Qaddafi is killed in Libya
events.summary: Rebels capture and kill him in his hometown after 42 years in power.
events.description:
On October 20, 2011, Muammar al-Qaddafi, who had ruled Libya since seizing power in a military coup on September 1, 1969, was captured and killed by rebel fighters in Sirte, his birthplace and one of the last towns still loyal to him.

Rebel forces had taken most of the capital, Tripoli, on August 22 and 23, and Qaddafi had evaded capture for several weeks.

sources.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica - Muammar al-Qaddafi
Encyclopaedia Britannica - Libya: Qaddafi toppled and killed

events.title: NASA's OSIRIS-REx grabs a sample from asteroid Bennu
events.summary: The spacecraft touches the asteroid for about six seconds, 200 million miles away.
events.description:
On October 20, 2020, NASA's OSIRIS-REx spacecraft briefly touched the surface of the asteroid Bennu, more than 200 million miles (321 million kilometres) from Earth, to collect dust and rock. It touched down within about one metre of its target at a site called Nightingale.

The sampling head was in contact for about six seconds. A burst of nitrogen gas stirred up surface material, and the spacecraft spent about five of those seconds collecting it.

sources.name: NASA - OSIRIS-REx TAGs Surface of Asteroid Bennu

events.title: A coal-waste landslide engulfs a school in Aberfan
events.summary: 116 children and 28 adults die when a spoil tip collapses on a Welsh village.
events.description:
On October 21, 1966, after heavy rain, a spoil tip from the Merthyr Vale Colliery above the Welsh village of Aberfan gave way. A slide of liquefied debris flowed down the mountainside at more than 80 miles per hour and smashed into Pantglas Junior School.

The disaster killed 144 people, 116 of them children. A public inquiry blamed the National Coal Board, whose chairman had claimed the slide could not have been foreseen, even though safety concerns had often been raised.

sources.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica - Aberfan disaster

events.title: Magellan's ships enter the strait that will bear his name
events.summary: The passage to the Pacific takes his fleet more than five weeks.
events.description:
On October 21, 1520, Ferdinand Magellan's fleet entered the strait at the southern tip of South America that is now named after him. The ships emerged into the ocean beyond on November 28, and Magellan is credited with naming it the Pacific.

Magellan was killed on Mactan in the Philippines on April 27, 1521, but one of his ships, under Juan Sebastián del Cano, sailed on to Spain, completing the first circumnavigation of Earth.

sources.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica - Ferdinand Magellan

events.title: My Fair Lady premieres in New York
events.summary: Audrey Hepburn stars, but another singer provides her voice.
events.description:
On October 21, 1964, the film My Fair Lady had its world premiere at New York's Criterion Theatre. Directed by George Cukor, it starred Audrey Hepburn as Eliza Doolittle and Rex Harrison as Henry Higgins, in an adaptation of Lerner and Loewe's stage musical based on George Bernard Shaw's play Pygmalion.

Studio executives judged Hepburn's singing unsuitable, so her songs were dubbed by Marni Nixon. The film won Academy Awards including best picture, best director and best actor for Harrison.

sources.name: American Film Institute Catalog - My Fair Lady (1964)

events.title: USS Constitution is launched in Boston
events.summary: The frigate later known as "Old Ironsides" is still in commission today.
events.description:
On October 21, 1797, the frigate Constitution was launched from Edmund Hartt's shipyard in Boston, one of the six original frigates of the new U.S. Navy. She first sailed on July 22, 1798.

In the War of 1812 she defeated four British frigates and earned the nickname "Old Ironsides." She remains the oldest commissioned warship afloat in the world.

sources.name: USS Constitution Museum - USS Constitution Facts
National Park Service - USS Constitution

events.title: Kennedy tells the nation about Soviet missiles in Cuba
events.summary: He announces a naval quarantine of the island.
events.description:
On October 22, 1962, President John F. Kennedy announced that the Soviet Union had placed offensive missiles in Cuba, which U.S. spy planes had photographed on October 14. He ordered a naval quarantine, saying the United States would stop and seize "offensive weapons and associated matériel" bound for the island.

On October 28 Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev agreed to remove the missiles. Kennedy promised not to invade Cuba and secretly promised to withdraw U.S. nuclear missiles from Turkey. The crisis was the closest the world had come to global nuclear war.

sources.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica - Cuban missile crisis

events.title: André-Jacques Garnerin makes the first parachute descent
events.summary: He drops from a balloon about 1,000 metres above Paris.
events.description:
On October 22, 1797, the French balloonist André-Jacques Garnerin jumped from a balloon about 1,000 metres (3,200 feet) above Parc Monceau in Paris and came down under an umbrella-shaped white canvas parachute about 7 metres across.

Garnerin became the first person to use a parachute regularly and successfully, and in 1802 he jumped from about 8,000 feet in England.

sources.name: Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum - Medal, André Jacques Garnerin
Encyclopaedia Britannica - André-Jacques Garnerin

events.title: Millerites wait in vain for the Second Coming
events.summary: The day their movement predicted for Christ's return passes without event.
events.description:
October 22, 1844, was the day followers of the American preacher William Miller expected Christ to return. Miller had predicted the Second Coming for around 1843, and when that passed, followers recalculated to October 22, 1844. The movement had an estimated 50,000 to 100,000 followers.

The day passed without event, an episode remembered as the Great Disappointment. Many believers concluded only the calculation was wrong, and the movement shaped later Adventist churches, including the Advent Christian Church and the Seventh-day Adventists.

sources.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica - Millerism

events.title: The College of New Jersey, later Princeton, receives its charter
events.summary: The colonial charter creates the college that will become Princeton University.
events.description:
On October 22, 1746, the College of New Jersey, which became Princeton University, received its charter, granted in the name of King George II by John Hamilton, acting governor of the province of New Jersey. The charter created a college "for the Education of Youth in the Learned Languages and in the Liberal Arts and Sciences."

Because Hamilton's authority was questioned, a second charter was issued in 1748 by the new governor, Jonathan Belcher.

sources.name: Princeton University Archives - It's Charter Day!
A Princeton Companion - Charter
